title: Thailand visa FAQ
summary: Short, clear answers to the questions we hear most about Thai visas: visa-free entry, the TDAC arrival card, visa runs, working on a DTV, Muay Thai visas and more.
seoTitle: Thailand Visa FAQ: Common Questions Answered
seoDescription: Do you need a visa for Thailand? What is TDAC? Can you work on a DTV or do a visa run? Plain-English answers to the most common Thai visa questions.

sections.heading: Quick answers, checked against official sources
paragraphs: These are the questions we are asked most often. Each answer is a short summary; follow the links to our visa pages for the full details, and always confirm with the official source or your Thai embassy before you travel. Thai rules change often, and the visa exemption changed on 15 September 2026.

faqs.q: Do I need a visa for Thailand?
faqs.a: It depends on your passport and your plans. From 15 September 2026, citizens of 54 countries and territories, including the UK, the US, Canada, Australia and most of the EU, can visit for up to 30 days for tourism without a visa. Some nationalities get 15 days, some get stays under bilateral agreements, and a few can get a Visa on Arrival. Everyone else, and anyone staying longer or coming to work, study or do business, needs a visa. Use our country checker to see your rule.

faqs.q: I entered on the old 60-day exemption. Do I have to leave early?
faqs.a: No. If you were admitted before 15 September 2026, you can stay until the date stamped in your passport. The new 30-day rule applies to entries on or after that date.

The Thailand Digital Arrival Card (TDAC) is the online arrival form that replaced the paper TM6 card. Every foreign traveller, including children, must complete it within three days before arriving. It is free at the official site, tdac.immigration.go.th. Sites that charge a fee are not official.

faqs.q: How do I apply for a Thai visa?
faqs.a: Almost all visas are applied for online at thaievisa.go.th, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs e-Visa portal. You apply from outside Thailand to the embassy for the country where you live, upload your documents and pay the fee online or as your embassy instructs. See our step-by-step e-Visa guide.

faqs.q: How long does my passport need to be valid?
faqs.a: At least six months from your arrival date, with blank pages for stamps. Airlines may refuse to board you if it is valid for less.

faqs.q: Can I extend my stay in Thailand?
faqs.a: Many visas can be extended once at a local immigration office, for a government fee of 1,900 THB. For example, a Tourist Visa's 60 days can usually be extended by 30 days, and a DTV entry by up to 180 days. Rules for extending a visa-exemption stay changed with the new scheme, so check with immigration before you rely on one.

faqs.q: Can I do a visa run?
faqs.a: A "visa run" means leaving Thailand and coming straight back to get a new stay. It is not illegal, but officers can refuse entry to people who seem to be living in Thailand on back-to-back exemptions, and entries by land on the visa exemption are limited. If you want to stay for months, a DTV, a Tourist Visa or another long-stay visa is the safer choice.

faqs.q: Can I work on a DTV?
faqs.a: You can work remotely for employers or clients outside Thailand. You cannot work for a Thai company or take a local job; that needs a work permit and usually a Non-Immigrant B visa.

faqs.q: Can I work remotely on a visa exemption or Tourist Visa?
faqs.a: These are tourism entries and they don't give permission to work. Answering the odd email on holiday is one thing; living and working in Thailand is another. If you work online while here, use the DTV or the LTR.

faqs.q: Which visa do I need for Muay Thai?
faqs.a: For a few weeks of training on holiday, the visa exemption or a Tourist Visa is usually enough. For longer stays, the Destination Thailand Visa (DTV) has a Muay Thai track that needs a camp letter and 500,000 THB in savings. The alternative is a Non-Immigrant ED visa sponsored by a licensed Muay Thai school. See our Muay Thai visa guide.

faqs.q: Can I visit Thailand for business meetings without a visa?
faqs.a: From 15 September 2026 the visa exemption is for tourism. If you are coming for meetings, conferences or other business, check with your Thai embassy whether you need a Non-Immigrant B (business) visa before you travel.

If you are 50 or older, look at the Non-Immigrant O (retirement) and Non-Immigrant O-A (long stay) visas, which need proof of funds or pension income. Wealthier retirees may also consider the LTR Wealthy Pensioner category or Thailand Privilege.

Overstaying is fined 500 THB per day, up to a maximum of 20,000 THB, and longer overstays can lead to bans on re-entering Thailand for years. If something goes wrong, go to an immigration office before your permitted stay ends.

faqs.q: What are TM30 and the 90-day report?
faqs.a: TM30 is the notice your landlord or hotel files to tell immigration where you are staying. The 90-day report is your own address report, due every 90 days if you stay that long in Thailand without leaving. Both apply to most long-stay visa holders.

faqs.q: Can you apply for my visa or check my documents?
faqs.a: No. We are an independent information site. We never ask for your passport details or payment for visas, and we can't review individual cases. Apply directly on thaievisa.go.th or contact your Thai embassy.
